notes.meaning: Here begins a list of the leading priests and Levites who came home from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua the high priest. (Levites were the tribe set apart to help in worship.) These men were the heads of the priestly groups that took turns serving at the temple, a system first set up by King David. Many think this Ezra and this Jeremiah are not the famous scribe and prophet. Others think this is the same Ezra, kept alive by God to a great age.

The list of priestly leaders goes on. Little more than their names is given. Even so, Scripture keeps them so that later people would remember the good men God used to bring worship back to life. One name, Abijah, is the family line that John the Baptist's father later came from.

The list closes with twenty-two chief priests in the days of Jeshua. They were descendants of Aaron and ranked just below the high priest. David had set up twenty-four groups. Two may have died out in Babylon, which could explain the smaller number. Their "associates" are fellow workers who helped them in the service.

Next come the chief Levites of that first return. Mattaniah and his helpers were in charge of the songs of thanksgiving. Their job was to make sure the psalms of praise were sung in the temple at the right times and in the right way. He was probably the leader of the first choir named in chapter 11.

Bakbukiah and Unni stood across from the other singers. This may mean the choirs stood facing each other in their places. Or it may mean they took turns serving in shifts. Matthew Henry pictures them relieving one another like brothers and fellow workers.

These verses trace the high priests from father to son, from Jeshua down to Jaddua. The list mattered because the Jews now had no king. They began to mark time by who was high priest. "Jonathan" is probably a copying slip for Johanan, named in verses 22-23. Many think Jaddua, or his father of the same name, was the high priest who later met Alexander the Great.

Now the list moves to the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Jeshua's son. The sons of the first priests took their fathers' places. Some fathers were still living, but many had died. Each priestly family is named after its founder, followed by its leader at that time. Matthew Henry sees God's care here: as one generation of ministers passes, God raises up another.

The same families from verses 1-7 appear again, with their new leaders. Some names are spelled a little differently. Malluchi is Malluch, Shebaniah is Shecaniah, Harim is Rehum, and Meraioth is Meremoth. These small changes likely came from copying by hand over many years.

Zichri led the family of Abijah. Later, Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist, came from this family. The leader for Miniamin's family is not named, and the family of Hattush is missing from this second list. One suggestion is that some of these men had no sons to carry on the line.

The list of family heads under Joiakim ends. Matthew Henry calls it a rare thing: twenty good fathers leaving behind twenty good sons to fill their places. It is good to know what our godly ancestors were like, so we learn what we should be.

The family heads of the Levites and priests kept being recorded through the time of four later high priests. Most of the older commentators take "Darius the Persian" to be the second Persian king of that name. One older writer, quoted by Adam Clarke, thought it was the last Persian king, who was beaten by Alexander the Great. Matthew Henry notes that in Eliashib's time many priests grew careless, but the Levites served all the more eagerly.

The Levite family heads were written down in "the Book of the Chronicles." This means the official public records where family lines were carefully kept. It is not the book of Chronicles in our Bible, which has no such list. That record has since been lost.

Hashabiah, Sherebiah and Jeshua led the Levites. Their fellow Levites stood across from them in choirs, taking turns to sing praise and thanks to God. This was done just as David, "the man of God," had commanded long before. Faithful worship was being restored in the old, God-given way.
